Technical Details and Algorithms

Siyang Ni

2025-11-13

Source: vignettes/technical-details.Rmd
technical-details.Rmd

Introduction

This vignette provides technical details on the statistical methods and algorithms implemented in surveymixr. It covers:

  • Growth mixture modeling framework
  • Complex survey design integration
  • EM algorithm implementation
  • Standard error computation
  • Bootstrap likelihood ratio test (BLRT)
  • Model fit indices

For an introduction to using the package, see vignette("surveymixr-intro").

Statistical Framework

Growth Mixture Models

Growth mixture models (GMMs) combine growth curve modeling with latent class analysis to identify distinct subgroups (classes) with different developmental trajectories (Muthén and Shedden 1999).

Individual-Level Model

For individual ii in class kk at time tt:

yit|k∼N(μitk,σk2)y_{it} | k \sim N(\mu_{itk}, \sigma^2_k)

where the mean trajectory is:

μitk=β0k+β1k⋅timeit+β2k⋅timeit2+⋯\mu_{itk} = \beta_{0k} + \beta_{1k} \cdot time_{it} + \beta_{2k} \cdot time_{it}^2 + \cdots

Class Membership

The probability that individual ii belongs to class kk:

P(Ci=k|𝐗i)=exp(γk0+γkT𝐗i)∑j=1Kexp(γj0+γjT𝐗i)P(C_i = k | \mathbf{X}_i) = \frac{\exp(\gamma_{k0} + \gamma_k^T \mathbf{X}_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^K \exp(\gamma_{j0} + \gamma_j^T \mathbf{X}_i)}

where 𝐗i\mathbf{X}_i are time-invariant covariates (optional).

Complex Survey Design Features

Survey data often involve:

  1. Stratification: Population divided into strata, samples drawn from each
  2. Clustering: Multi-stage sampling (e.g., schools, then students)
  3. Unequal probability weights: Some units more likely to be sampled

Survey-Weighted Likelihood

The survey-weighted log-likelihood is:

ℓw(θ)=∑i=1nwilogf(yi|θ)\ell_w(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i \log f(y_i | \theta)

where wiw_i is the survey weight for individual ii.

Key innovation: surveymixr integrates survey weights directly into the EM algorithm, unlike post-hoc weighting approaches.

Integration: Survey-Weighted GMM

Combining GMM with survey design:

ℓw(θ)=∑i=1nwilog[∑k=1Kπk∏t=1Tif(yit|θk)]\ell_w(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i \log \left[ \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k \prod_{t=1}^{T_i} f(y_{it} | \theta_k) \right]

where: - wiw_i = survey weight - πk\pi_k = class proportion (weighted) - θk\theta_k = class-specific parameters - TiT_i = number of observations for individual ii

Estimation Algorithm

EM Algorithm Overview

The Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm (Dempster, Laird, and Rubin 1977) iterates between:

  1. E-step: Compute posterior class probabilities
  2. M-step: Update parameters given posterior probabilities

E-Step: Posterior Probabilities

For individual ii and class kk:

τik=wiπk∏t=1Tif(yit|θk)∑j=1Kwiπj∏t=1Tif(yit|θj)\tau_{ik} = \frac{w_i \pi_k \prod_{t=1}^{T_i} f(y_{it} | \theta_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K w_i \pi_j \prod_{t=1}^{T_i} f(y_{it} | \theta_j)}

where τik=P(Ci=k|yi,θ)\tau_{ik} = P(C_i = k | y_i, \theta) is the posterior probability.

M-Step: Parameter Updates

Class proportions (weighted):

πk=∑i=1nwiτik∑i=1nwi\pi_k = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n w_i \tau_{ik}}{\sum_{i=1}^n w_i}

Growth parameters (class kk):

Solve weighted regression:

β̂k=argminβk∑i=1n∑t=1Tiwiτik(yit−𝐗itTβk)2\hat{\beta}_k = \arg\min_{\beta_k} \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{t=1}^{T_i} w_i \tau_{ik} (y_{it} - \mathbf{X}_{it}^T \beta_k)^2

Variance (class kk):

σ̂k2=∑i=1n∑t=1Tiwiτik(yit−ŷit)2∑i=1n∑t=1Tiwiτik\hat{\sigma}^2_k = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{t=1}^{T_i} w_i \tau_{ik} (y_{it} - \hat{y}_{it})^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{t=1}^{T_i} w_i \tau_{ik}}

Convergence Criterion

Stop when:

|ℓw(t+1)−ℓw(t)|<ϵ|\ell_w^{(t+1)} - \ell_w^{(t)}| < \epsilon

Default: ϵ=10−6\epsilon = 10^{-6}

Missing Data Handling (FIML)

surveymixr uses Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) for missing data under the Missing at Random (MAR) assumption.

For individual ii with observed data yiobsy_i^{obs}:

ℓw(θ|yiobs)=∑k=1Kwiτiklog∏t∈obsif(yit|θk)\ell_w(\theta | y_i^{obs}) = \sum_{k=1}^K w_i \tau_{ik} \log \prod_{t \in obs_i} f(y_{it} | \theta_k)

Advantages: - Uses all available data - Unbiased under MAR - No need for imputation

Multiple Random Starts

Local maxima are common in mixture models. surveymixr uses multiple random starts:

  1. Generate starts (default 500) random initial parameter values
  2. Run EM from each starting point (parallelized)
  3. Select solution with highest log-likelihood
  4. Check for local maxima with diagnose_convergence()

Example:

fit <- gmm_survey(
  data = mcs_simulated,
  id = "id",
  time = "age",
  outcome = "selfcontrol",
  n_classes = 3,
  starts = 500,  # Multiple random starts
  cores = 4      # Parallel processing
)

# Check for local maxima
diagnose_convergence(fit)

Standard Errors

Sandwich Estimator

surveymixr uses the sandwich (robust) variance estimator to account for: - Model misspecification - Clustering - Stratification

𝐕(θ̂)=𝐇−1𝐉𝐇−1\mathbf{V}(\hat{\theta}) = \mathbf{H}^{-1} \mathbf{J} \mathbf{H}^{-1}

where: - 𝐇\mathbf{H} = Hessian (observed information matrix) - 𝐉\mathbf{J} = Outer product of score contributions (meat)

Accounting for Survey Design

Clustering adjustment:

𝐉=∑h=1H∑c=1Ch(∑i∈c𝐬i)(∑i∈c𝐬i)T\mathbf{J} = \sum_{h=1}^H \sum_{c=1}^{C_h} \left(\sum_{i \in c} \mathbf{s}_i\right) \left(\sum_{i \in c} \mathbf{s}_i\right)^T

where: - HH = number of strata - ChC_h = number of clusters in stratum hh - 𝐬i\mathbf{s}_i = score contribution for individual ii

Effect: Standard errors increase to reflect within-cluster correlation (design effect > 1).

Numerical Derivatives

Since analytical derivatives are complex, surveymixr uses numerical derivatives via the numDeriv package:

  • Hessian: Richardson extrapolation
  • Gradient: Central differences

Confidence intervals:

θ̂±1.96×SE(θ̂)\hat{\theta} \pm 1.96 \times SE(\hat{\theta})

Bootstrap Likelihood Ratio Test (BLRT)

The BLRT (McLachlan 1987) tests whether a kk-class model fits better than a (k−1)(k-1)-class model.

Algorithm

  1. Fit (k−1)(k-1)-class model, obtain θ̂k−1\hat{\theta}_{k-1}
  2. Fit kk-class model, obtain θ̂k\hat{\theta}_k
  3. Compute observed LRT statistic: LRTobs=2(ℓ(θ̂k)−ℓ(θ̂k−1))LRT_{obs} = 2(\ell(\hat{\theta}_k) - \ell(\hat{\theta}_{k-1}))
  4. Bootstrap (repeat BB times):
    • Simulate data from (k−1)(k-1)-class model
    • Fit both (k−1)(k-1) and kk-class models
    • Compute LRTbLRT_b
  5. pp-value = proportion of LRTb>LRTobsLRT_b > LRT_{obs}

Interpretation: - p<0.05p < 0.05: Reject (k−1)(k-1) classes, favor kk classes - p≥0.05p \geq 0.05: No evidence for kk classes

Example:

selection <- gmm_select(
  data = mcs_simulated,
  id = "id",
  time = "age",
  outcome = "selfcontrol",
  min_classes = 1,
  max_classes = 5,
  run_blrt = TRUE,
  blrt_samples = 500,  # Bootstrap replicates
  cores = 4
)

# View BLRT results
summary(selection)

Model Fit Indices

Information Criteria

AIC (Akaike Information Criterion):

AIC=−2ℓ(θ̂)+2pAIC = -2\ell(\hat{\theta}) + 2p

BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion):

BIC=−2ℓ(θ̂)+plog(n)BIC = -2\ell(\hat{\theta}) + p \log(n)

Sample-size adjusted BIC:

aBIC=−2ℓ(θ̂)+plog(n+224)aBIC = -2\ell(\hat{\theta}) + p \log\left(\frac{n+2}{24}\right)

where: - ℓ(θ̂)\ell(\hat{\theta}) = maximized log-likelihood - pp = number of parameters - nn = sample size (effective sample size for weighted data)

Lower values indicate better fit.

Entropy

Entropy measures classification certainty (Ramaswamy et al. 1993):

E=1−∑i=1n∑k=1Kτiklog(τik)nlog(K)E = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{k=1}^K \tau_{ik} \log(\tau_{ik})}{n \log(K)}

  • Range: [0,1][0, 1]
  • Higher values = better classification
  • E>0.8E > 0.8 is considered good
  • E>0.9E > 0.9 is excellent

Average Posterior Probability (AvePP)

For each class kk:

AvePPk=∑i:argmaxjτij=kτiknkAvePP_k = \frac{\sum_{i: \arg\max_j \tau_{ij} = k} \tau_{ik}}{n_k}

where nkn_k = number of individuals assigned to class kk.

Interpretation: - AvePP > 0.7 for all classes is acceptable - AvePP > 0.8 is good

Odds of Correct Classification (OCC)

OCCk=AvePPk/(1−AvePPk)πk/(1−πk)OCC_k = \frac{AvePP_k / (1 - AvePP_k)}{\pi_k / (1 - \pi_k)}

where πk\pi_k = class proportion.

  • OCC > 5 indicates good classification

Computational Efficiency

Parallelization

Random starts are parallelized using the parallel package:

# Detect cores
n_cores <- parallel::detectCores() - 1

fit <- gmm_survey(
  ...,
  cores = n_cores
)

Memory Management

For large datasets: - Use sparse matrices where applicable - Process data in chunks for FIML - Limit random starts for initial exploration

Typical Run Times

On a modern laptop (4 cores):

n T K starts Time
1,000 4 2 100 ~1 min
1,000 4 3 500 ~5 min
5,000 6 3 500 ~15 min
10,000 6 4 1000 ~45 min

Tips for speed: 1. Start with fewer random starts (50-100) for exploration 2. Use parallel processing (4+ cores) 3. Reduce to final model with more starts (500-1000)

References

Dempster, Arthur P, Nan M Laird, and Donald B Rubin. 1977. “Maximum Likelihood from Incomplete Data via the EM Algorithm.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Methodological) 39 (1): 1–22.
McLachlan, Geoffrey J. 1987. “On Bootstrapping the Likelihood Ratio Test Statistic for the Number of Components in a Normal Mixture.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series C (Applied Statistics) 36 (3): 318–24.
Muthén, Bengt, and Kerby Shedden. 1999. “Finite Mixture Modeling with Mixture Outcomes Using the EM Algorithm.” Biometrics 55 (2): 463–69.
Ramaswamy, Venkatram, Wayne S DeSarbo, David J Reibstein, and William T Robinson. 1993. “An Empirical Pooling Approach for Estimating Marketing Mix Elasticities with PIMS Data.” Marketing Science 12 (1): 103–24.
